food.text: Peruvian cuisine has seen a revival of interest in native foods and techniques in recent decades, with quinoa, kiwicha, chili peppers and several roots and tubers growing more popular. Chef Gastón Acurio has become well known for raising awareness of local ingredients.

The most important ingredient in Peruvian cuisine is the potato, and Peru has the widest variety of potatoes in the world. Potatoes and other tubers are one of four traditional staples, alongside corn, Amaranthaceae such as quinoa, kañiwa and kiwicha, and legumes.

Paisa cuisine of the Colombian Andes leans on beans, rice, maize, pork, beef and potatoes. Its signature bandeja paisa combines carne asada or carne molida, chicharrón, rice, red beans, avocado, sweet fried plantains, a fried egg and a small white corn arepa. The dish is also popular in Colombian restaurants in Europe and the United States.

In 2004 the Peruvian government launched the "Gastronomy Project" to promote the country's culinary traditions and encourage the development of its restaurant industry. Among the most distinguishable ingredients of Peruvian cuisine are aji amarillo peppers, huacatay herb and Peruvian corn.

Physalis peruviana, whose cultivation in South America can be traced to the Inca Empire, was widely introduced elsewhere in the 20th century. It is now cultivated or grows wild across temperate and tropical regions, and has become invasive in some habitats, particularly in Hawaii.

Changua, a milk soup with eggs, is a typical breakfast in the central Andes of Colombia, including Boyacá, Cundinamarca, Santander and Bogotá. The dish has Chibcha origins and is served with curly cilantro and a piece of hard bread called calado, which is softened in the broth.

Colombian coffee is known for its quality and distinct flavor, yet many Colombians commonly drink instant coffee rather than brewed. It is popularly consumed as a tinto, black with sugar or panela on the side, or as café con leche. In 2011 UNESCO declared the Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia a World Heritage Site.

In 2008 the Peruvian government declared June 28 "National Ceviche Day" in recognition of the dish's importance to Peruvian cuisine. The declaration came four years after the government launched its 2004 "Gastronomy Project" to promote the country's culinary traditions.

Peruvians line up at bakeries for freshly baked white bread from 6 to 9 am and from 4 to 6 pm, and most eat bread for breakfast with coffee or tea. Almost all bread except baguettes is fortified with added fats such as lard, and whole wheat bread is extremely hard to find in major cities.
In Peru, Physalis peruviana is called aguaymanto in Spanish and topotopo in Quechua. In Colombia it goes by its Aymara name uchuva, and in Ecuador it is called uvilla, Spanish for 'little grape'.

When Lanín National Park was created in 1937, new roads connected San Martín de los Andes in Argentina with the rest of the country. The resulting increase in trade almost ended local husbandry and agriculture, and tourism later became the main industry.

A few bakeries in coastal Peruvian cities produce "bollos," loaves of bread baked in stone and wood ovens from the Andes. Authentic whole wheat bread, by contrast, is imported from Europe and sold at upscale grocery stores, though whole wheat is more common and often cheaper in rural towns.

art.text: The Crown of the Andes was made in Popayán, Colombia, for a statue of the Virgin Mary and is adorned with 450 emeralds. Its owners sought papal permission to sell it in the early decades of the 20th century, and it was sold in 1936 to an American syndicate. It now belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City.

Beatriz González was a Colombian painter, sculptor, critic, curator and art historian, often associated with pop art. She grew up in the 1940s and 1950s, when Colombia was plagued with violence and war during La Violencia, and she was best known for her bright, colorful paintings depicting life in Colombia in that war-torn period.

Peruvian architecture in the 20th century is characterized by eclecticism, which constructive functionalism has stood against. The most considerable example is Plaza San Martín in Lima. In 1988 UNESCO declared Lima's historical center a world heritage site, inspiring many laws to protect the city's buildings.

When Chicago businessman Warren J. Piper led the syndicate that bought the Crown of the Andes in 1936, he said it would be broken up and the jewels sold individually. That did not happen, and the crown was instead exhibited sporadically over the next few decades. Papal permission for the sale had been granted back in 1914.

In 1965 Beatriz González painted The Suicides of Sisga, based on a newspaper photo of a young couple who had a professional photographer take their portrait before jumping off the Sisga dam to their deaths. The two young farmers were deeply in love, and the man, who was suspected to be mentally insane, convinced his girlfriend to commit suicide to show their religious devotion and to preserve the purity of their love. The Salon of Colombian Artists jury first dismissed the painting as a "bad Botero", but after Marta Traba pressed them it was accepted and won a special prize.

In 1985 Beatriz González's work shifted from vibrant colors and shapes to darker imagery after the M-19 guerrilla attack on the Palace of Justice, carried out in an attempt to put the President of Colombia on trial. The attack left 94 dead. Feeling she could not laugh after that event, she began to explore themes of death and the drug trade, and some of Colombia's most tragic events.

The School of Fine Arts of Lima was founded in 1919, a milestone for Peruvian sculpture and painting. José Sabogal led the indigenist movement, which became a pillar of contemporary Peruvian painting.
tags: School of Fine Arts of Lima

art.text: In 1937 General Motors used the Crown of the Andes at the unveiling of its new Chevrolet models in Detroit. About 225,000 people are said to have viewed it, some 15% of the city's population. It was also shown at the 1939 New York World's Fair.

After the Metropolitan Museum announced its acquisition of the Crown of the Andes in December 2015, Colombia's Instituto Distrital de Cultura y Turismo suggested it should return to the region where it has the most cultural significance. The crown was made in Popayán from local gold and emeralds and used there in worship for three centuries.
tags: Instituto Distrital de Cultura y Turismo

art.text: Although often labeled a pop artist, Beatriz González never considered herself one. She said she saw herself as a painter who painted "the joy of the underdeveloped", making a provincial art without horizons that confronted the everyday.

Beatriz González graduated from the fine arts department of the University of Los Andes in 1962. There she studied under the Argentine critic Marta Traba and the Spanish painter Joan Antonio Roda. She credited Traba with encouraging the presence of women in the Colombian art scene.

Reconstructions of some Muisca houses (bohíos) and of their most important temple, the Temple of the Sun in Sogamoso, were built in the second half of the 20th century. The Muisca themselves used only wood and clay, and the Spanish conquerors destroyed all the original houses and temples.

The Crown of the Andes was sold at a Sotheby auction in London in 1963 to the Dutch diamond company Asscher, acting for an anonymous buyer. It later came to the jeweler Oscar Heyman, who gave it to his daughter Alice Heyman, a founding member of the Women's Bank of New York City.

war.text: The Chaco War was fought from 1932 to 1935 between Bolivia and Paraguay over the northern Gran Chaco, which was thought to be rich in petroleum. It was the first war in South America to use modern weapons such as machine guns, armoured fighting vehicles and airplanes.

The Chaco War was the bloodiest South American war of the 20th century. Bolivia lost between 56,000 and 65,000 people, 2% of its population, and Paraguay lost about 36,000, or 3% of its population. Thousands more suffered non-combat deaths from dehydration, mostly among Bolivian troops, in a semi-arid land that earned the conflict the name "The War of Thirst".

The Ecuadorian–Peruvian War, known locally as the War of '41, was fought from 5 July to 2 October 1941. Peru occupied the Ecuadorian province of El Oro and parts of Loja. Although it happened during World War II, neither country was supported by the Allies or the Axis.

Bolivia had a larger and better-equipped army and income from mining. Even so, problems with international trade and poor internal communications turned the tide against it. The war ended at the Chaco Peace Conference in Buenos Aires in July 1938, which awarded three-quarters of the Gran Chaco to Paraguay.

Bolivia's Isla de la Luna in Lake Titicaca was used by the Bolivian Ministry of the Interior as a detention center for political prisoners in the 20th century, and came to be known as the Alcatraz of the Andes. Its 30-foot adobe walls were built between 1932 and 1935 by Paraguayan prisoners of war during the Chaco War. Escape was believed nearly impossible because the lake's ice-cold water would kill even a skilled swimmer with hypothermia.

Communist revolutionary Ernesto "Che" Guevara was captured and executed by Bolivian soldiers on October 9, 1967. He and his Cuban followers had studied Quechua to reach Bolivian peasants, but the Chiriguanos where he operated spoke Guarani. In 2005 the Guarani created a 300-kilometre "Trail of Che Guevara" for tourists.

The Battle of Ybybobó began on 28 December 1934 and lasted until early January 1935. Paraguayan forces isolated some of the Bolivian troops on the Pilcomayo River, killing 200 of them and taking 1,200 prisoner, while the Paraguayans lost only a few dozen men. Some fleeing Bolivian soldiers were reported to have jumped into the fast-flowing waters of the Pilcomayo River to avoid capture.

In September 1949, Hernan Siles Zuazo, Emilio Sfeir and others escaped from Isla de la Luna and won political asylum in Peru. Ironically, both men had served in Bolivia's war effort in the Chaco War, Siles Zuazo as an infantry soldier and Sfeir as a counter-intelligence agent.

A ceasefire took effect on 31 July 1941, but Peru soon broke it, and a new one ended the clashes on 2 October. Ecuador and Peru signed the Rio Protocol on 29 January 1942. Their border disputes were not fully resolved until the Cenepa War of 1995 and the Brasilia Presidential Act of October 1998.

Colombia severed relations with Peru in February 1933 over the Leticia dispute, and the two countries fought each other. The fighting lasted until President Luis Miguel Sánchez Cerro was assassinated the same year by an APRA member.

In September 1932 the Argentine Army set up a special detachment at Formosa Province, called Destacamento Mixto Formosa, to deal with deserters from both sides trying to cross into Argentine territory. By the end of the Chaco War, 15,000 Bolivian soldiers had deserted to Argentina. The source also says 10,000 Bolivian troops, many of them ill-trained and ill-equipped conscripts, deserted to Argentina or injured or mutilated themselves to avoid combat.

On November 2, 1972, between 50 and 60 political prisoners escaped from Isla de la Luna and reached Peru. They had been detained by General Hugo Banzer's government after the August 1972 coup against General Juan Jose Torres.

literature.text: Peruvian literature began in the oral traditions of pre-Columbian civilizations. In the early 20th century, the Indigenismo movement produced writers such as Ciro Alegría, José María Arguedas and César Vallejo. In the second half of the century, Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa became a leading member of the Latin American Boom.

Piers Paul Read's 1974 book Alive told the story of Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571, which crashed in the Andes on 13 October 1972. Of the 45 people aboard, only 16 survived 72 days of sub-zero temperatures. With little food in the wrecked fuselage and facing starvation, the survivors realized they would have to eat the frozen bodies of the dead. Newsweek's Walter Clemons said the book would become a classic in the literature of survival.
literature.source_title: Alive: The Story of the Andes Survivors

literature.text: The 1953 Newbery Medal went to Secret of the Andes, a children's novel by Ann Nolan Clark, illustrated by Jean Charlot. It follows Cusi, a modern Inca boy who leaves his home high in the Andes with his pet llama, Misti, to learn the secret of his ancestors.

Colombian LGBTQ literature dates back to the early 20th century and the homoerotic poetry of Porfirio Barba-Jacob. The first openly homosexual Colombian novel, Por los caminos de Sodoma: confesiones íntimas de un homosexual, was published in Buenos Aires in 1932 by Bernardo Arias Trujillo under the pseudonym Sir Edgar Dixon. It was rejected at the time because of its subject matter, though it is now considered a landmark in Latin American LGBT literature.

In Mario Vargas Llosa's 1993 novel Death in the Andes, Corporal Lituma in the mountain town of Naccos investigates the disappearances of three men. His lack of understanding of Indigenous Andean culture, including apus, pishtacos and mukis, is a significant obstacle. In the end Lituma becomes convinced, and a former worker bitterly confirms, that the townspeople sacrificed the three men to the local apus to protect themselves from terrucos, landslides and the closing of the construction site. They ate the men's testicles, a taste the worker says he can never wash out of his mouth.

Secret of the Andes is now remembered for beating E. B. White's Charlotte's Web, a runner-up in 1953. One Newbery committee member said she voted for it because she hadn't seen any good books about South America. Anita Silvey later wrote that Secret of the Andes is a good book, but Charlotte's Web the best.

Piers Paul Read said he was tempted to fictionalize parts of Alive for dramatic impact, but decided the bare facts were enough. When he returned in October 1973 with the manuscript, some survivors felt the faith and friendship that inspired them in the cordillera did not emerge from its pages.
literature.source_title: Alive: The Story of the Andes Survivors

literature.text: Fernando Vallejo's autobiographical series El río del tiempo includes El fuego secreto, published in 1987, in which he explores drug use and homosexuality as an adolescent in the cities of Medellín and Bogotá. Recurrent themes in most of his work include violence, homosexuality, adolescence, drugs, death and the defense of animal rights. His La virgen de los sicarios, translated as Our Lady of the Assassins, also deals with LGBTQ themes.

Fernando Vallejo wrote the biography of poet Porfirio Barba-Jacob as a novel, El mensajero, in 1987. Barba-Jacob lived his homosexuality openly and wrote of love between men in his poems, many of them written while living in exile outside Colombia, a country where he always had many followers and a great influence.

Bernardo Arias Trujillo wrote the poem Roby Nelson, about the beauty of an Argentine boy. It became very popular and is still an example of homosexual literature not only in Colombia but throughout Latin America.

In 2017, Pablo Landeo wrote the first novel in Quechua without a Spanish translation. In 2019, Roxana Quispe Collantes of the University of San Marcos defended the first thesis in the language group, on the works of poet Andrés Alencastre Gutiérrez.

In 1982, President Fernando Belaúnde Terry asked Mario Vargas Llosa to join the Investigatory Commission, a task force to inquire into the massacre of eight journalists at the hands of the villagers of Uchuraccay. That experience inspired Who Killed Palomino Molero? and Death in the Andes.

Most 20th century Quechua literature consists of traditional folk stories and oral narratives, though dramas, poems and more prose were also published. Johnny Payne has translated two sets of Quechua oral short stories, one into Spanish and the other into English.

Pablo Vierci's 2008 book Society of the Snow became the basis for J. A. Bayona's film. Vierci wrote that, contrary to what apocalyptic fiction predicts, the 'every man for himself' scenario did not happen among the Andes survivors, and that solidarity arose instead.

science.text: The Perito Moreno Glacier, fed by the Southern Patagonian Ice Field in the Andes, closed its Rico arm for the first time in 1917, followed by the first break. Ruptures of the resulting ice dam were then recorded in 1935, 1940 and many later years, up to 2019.

The Perito Moreno Glacier covers 250 km2 and is 30 km long. It is one of 48 glaciers fed by the Southern Patagonian Ice Field in the Andes system, which is the world's third largest reserve of fresh water.

The Andean plant Physalis peruviana was widely introduced around the world in the 20th century. It is now cultivated or grows wild across temperate and tropical regions, and it has become invasive in some natural habitats, forming thickets, particularly in Hawaii and on other Pacific islands. Its unripe raw fruits, flowers, leaves and stems contain solanine and solanidine alkaloids that may cause poisoning if ingested by humans, cattle or horses.

Tree rings on the shorelines of the Brazo Rico show that there were no major damming and rupture events there from about 1635 until the 20th century. The front of the Perito Moreno Glacier began moving toward the opposite bank at the end of the 19th century, and it closed the arm in 1917.

The center of genetic diversity of Physalis peruviana is in the Andes Mountains of Ecuador, Chile, Colombia and Peru. Dozens of ecotypes are believed to exist, and wild forms are thought to have 2n = 24 chromosomes, while cultivated forms include varieties with 32 or 48 chromosomes.

Today most dogs in South America are of European descent, and the only indigenous breed is the Peruvian Hairless dog. Free-ranging dogs are mostly descended from European dogs, but they carry traces of pre-Columbian dog DNA.

The University of the Andes in Bogotá was founded in 1948 by Colombian intellectuals led by Mario Laserna Pinzón. It was the first Colombian university established as nonsectarian, and it now teaches medicine, engineering, science and law. It also runs a joint academic venture with the Santa Fe de Bogotá Foundation, a medical institution.

In 2004 the dammed lake behind the Perito Moreno Glacier peaked at a level of 10.5 m, and the discharge flow peaked at 5000 m³ / s. Lake levels matched again after four days, and an estimated 10,000 tourists watched the event.

In 2005, Colonel John Blashford-Snell confirmed in Bolivia the existence of the double-nosed Andean tiger hound. These dogs may have descended from the Pachón Navarro, a Spanish breed of hunting dog that occasionally shows a double nose.

Universidad de los Andes in Santiago was founded on September 8, 1989. Its faculty of law began in 1990, followed by the medical faculty. It was the first private Chilean university outside the Council of Chancellors to teach medicine, and its campus houses the CiiB, the Center for Research and Biomedical Innovation.

The 2008 rupture at the Perito Moreno Glacier had a peak discharge of 8000 m³ / s and ended after about four days. The 2012 event peaked at only 2000 m³ / s, so the accumulated water took longer to drain, finishing after 14 days.

In October 1996 the Rico arm rose about a meter, and by the end of the month water pressure opened a passage in the glacial front. The passage was not wide enough, so discharge was slow, peaking at 123 m³ / s at the end of January. Levels equalized only at the beginning of April.

politics.text: The Movement Towards Socialism, known as MAS, was democratically elected to govern Bolivia in December 2005 under Evo Morales. It stayed the incumbent party until the 2025 Bolivian general election.

The rainbow flag is often displayed in Peru and Bolivia as a symbol of Inca heritage, but Peruvian historiography holds that the Inca Empire never had a flag. Peruvian historian María Rostworowski said she would bet her life that no such flag ever existed.

The Unión Revolucionaria was founded in 1931 by Luis Miguel Sánchez Cerro as the official party of his regime. Sánchez Cerro was not a fascist himself but admired Benito Mussolini. His party adopted some symbols from Mussolini's followers, such as the blackshirt attire.

Felipe Quispe founded the Tupac Katari Guerrilla Army in 1989. Even with Quispe imprisoned, the group was involved in violent incidents until 1995. The article gives no details of who was attacked or how many were hurt or killed.
Along Katarist lines, the MAS party evolved to support coca farmers, mine workers and the urban poor. Under Evo Morales, it drew on the concept of a "pre-european colonial utopia".

After Sánchez Cerro's assassination in 1933, Luis A. Flores led the Unión Revolucionaria and tried to set up a Blackshirt movement on the Italian model. He returned from a nine-year exile in 1945 and resumed his fascist advocacy despite the end of the war. In 1949 he was named ambassador to Italy.

Peruvian president Alejandro Toledo, who served from 2001 to 2006, flew the rainbow flag at Lima's presidential palace. The city of Cusco also flies it, though as an official flag of the city rather than an Inca emblem.

Felipe Quispe was released from prison in 1997. He then reinvigorated the CSUTCB, the Unified Syndical Confederation of Peasant Workers of Bolivia, which had first formed in 1979 to represent Aymara people.
In the 1960s, peasant student activists and intellectuals in La Paz formed a group based on the ideology of Fausto Reinaga. Felipe Quispe later organised the group.

According to the newspaper El Comercio, the rainbow flag dates to the first decades of the 20th century. The Congress of the Republic of Peru has also declared the flag a fake, citing the conclusion of the National Academy of Peruvian History.
tags: Congress of the Republic of Peru

politics.text: Trujillo's municipality created the Trujillo Metropolitan Development Plan 2010, known as "Plandemetru", after two decades of disordered growth raised the cost of basic services. City ordinance approved it on November 30, 1995.

philosophy.text: Nicolás Gómez Dávila was a Colombian philosopher and aphorist, sometimes called the "Nietzsche of the Andes." He was a staunch critic of modernity. His work consists almost entirely of aphorisms that he called "escolios."

Fascism as a political philosophy held great influence in Peru during the early to mid-20th century. It grew strong after the Arequipa revolution of 1930 and declined after World War II. It drew mainly on Italian fascism, and to a lesser extent Spanish falangism, while also drawing on Catholic tradition and the concept of Mestizaje.

Gómez Dávila never attended a university, yet he built a library of more than 30,000 volumes, around which his literary life centred. In 1948 he helped found the University of the Andes in Bogotá. He spent most of his life among friends and books.

Gómez Dávila remained obscure until the last few years of his life, and he showed little interest in spreading his work widely. Then translations drew important attention, mainly in German-speaking countries. He died in 1994.

María del Rosario Casas Dupuy entered the University of the Andes in 1969, focusing on philosophy and literature. She was one of the top performing students of her class. She later became a professor of literary studies and philosophy at the Pontificia Universidad Javeriana and the National University of Colombia.

Gómez Dávila created "the reactionary" as his literary mask. He tried to place this figure beyond the traditional positions of left and right. His criticism of modernity rested on traditionalist Catholicism, influenced by Friedrich Nietzsche, and he saw himself as a partisan for a "truth that will not die."

The first volume of Gómez Dávila's works, Notas I, was published by his brother in 1954. Only 100 copies were printed, and they were given as gifts to his friends, so the book stayed virtually unknown. A second volume never appeared.

Peru's Constitution protects freedom of conscience and religion, and states there is no crime of opinion. Yet Article 50 recognizes the Catholic Church's role in the nation's moral development. An agreement signed with the Vatican in 1980 gives the Church special status in Peru.

Gómez Dávila followed Notas I in 1959 with a small book of essays, Textos I. These essays develop the basic concepts of his philosophical anthropology and his philosophy of history, often in literary language full of metaphors. His five volumes of Escolios a un texto implícito appeared from the seventies to the nineties.

The Universidad de los Andes in Santiago, Chile, is a private Catholic-inspired university founded on September 8, 1989. After its faculty of law began in 1990, the medical faculty and the institute of philosophy followed.

culture.text: Pagan rites from the pre-Columbian era are still common during the religious festivals of indigenous Bolivians. The festival clothing is reminiscent of the dress of pre-Columbian indigenous peoples and 16th century Spaniards.

Peruvians' beliefs are still heavily influenced by indigenous religious traditions. Catholicism, the largest religion in Peru, has absorbed Inca cultural traditions and indigenous beliefs and practices, and Indigenous Peruvians have blended it with their traditional beliefs.

Peru's official languages are Spanish, Quechua and Aymara. Around the start of the 21st century, about 50 languages were estimated to be spoken there, though Spanish is used by about 94.4% of the population and all types of Quechua combined by 13.9%.
The annual carnival of Oruro is counted among the great folkloric events of South America. Bolivia also holds the lesser known Anata Andina and the Pujllay carnival at Tarabuco.

Peru's national football team played at the FIFA World Cup in 1930, 1970, 1978 and 1982, and won the Copa América in 1939 and 1975. Teófilo Cubillas is the only player to score 5 goals in 2 different World Cups.

San Martín de los Andes, founded in 1898 as a military outpost, became a tourism town after Lanín National Park opened in 1937. It hosts the National Mountainman Festival and the Trabún Festival, both related to local culture.
The Tinku, a set of fertility rites, is held at Macha in Bolivia every 3 May. It is listed alongside other indigenous festivals, and Bolivians also celebrate Dia de los Muertos.
In 2003, the Peruvian club Cienciano won the Copa Sudamericana by defeating Argentinian club River Plate. It then beat Boca Juniors in the Recopa Sudamericana played in Miami.

Alex Olmedo, a tennis player from Peru with American citizenship, helped win the Davis Cup for the United States in 1958. In 1959 he won two Majors, in Australia and at Wimbledon, and he was inducted into the Tennis Hall of Fame in 1987.
